Products containing multivalent cations can impair the absorption of tetracyclines, potentially reducing their efficacy. It is recommended to separate the administration of tetracyclines from these products. 2. Magnesium hydroxide reduces the levels of oxytetracycline by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Alternative drugs should be considered, or close monitoring should be implemented. 3. Magnesium hydroxide decreases the effects of pancrelipase through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Antacids may negate the beneficial effects of enzymes. Caution is advised, and close monitoring is necessary. 4. Paromomycin increases the renal clearance of magnesium hydroxide, thereby reducing its levels. This interaction is considered minor, and its clinical significance is unknown. 5. Magnesium hydroxide reduces the levels or effects of pazopanib by increasing gastric pH. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Co-administration of pazopanib with drugs that raise gastric pH should be avoided. Short-acting antacids may be used as an alternative to proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) and H2 antagonists, but pazopanib and antacid dosing should be separated by several hours. 6. Magnesium hydroxide decreases the levels of penicillamine by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Administration should be separated by at least 2 hours, and close monitoring is recommended. 7. Magnesium hydroxide reduces the levels or effects of pexidartinib by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Therapy should be modified, and administration of pexidartinib should be separated by 2 hours before or after taking a locally-acting antacid. 8. Mineral oil decreases the levels of phenindione by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown. 9. Magnesium hydroxide reduces the levels of ponatinib by increasing gastric pH. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Alternative drugs should be considered, and co-administration should be avoided. 10. Magnesium hydroxide decreases the effects of potassium phosphates (IV) by cation binding in the gastrointestinal tract. Magnesium also reduces serum phosphate concentrations by binding dietary phosphate. Alternative therapies should be used if available. 11. Mineral oil decreases the levels of protamine by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown. 12. Magnesium hydroxide reduces the levels or effects of raltegravir by cation binding in the gastrointestinal tract. Magnesium-containing antacids lower raltegravir plasma levels when taken within 6 hours of the raltegravir dose. Co-administration should be avoided, and close monitoring is required. 13. Magnesium hydroxide decreases the levels of riociguat by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Administration should be separated by at least 1 hour, and close monitoring is recommended. 14. Magnesium hydroxide reduces the levels or effects of sarecycline by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Therapy should be modified, and close monitoring is required. Administration of sarecycline should be separated from multivalent cation-containing products. 15. Magnesium hydroxide decreases the effects of sodium phosphates (IV) by cation binding in the gastrointestinal tract. Magnesium also reduces serum phosphate concentrations by binding dietary phosphate. Alternative therapies should be used if available. 16. Sodium polystyrene sulfonate increases the levels of magnesium hydroxide by decreasing renal clearance. This interaction is considered minor, but there is a risk of alkalosis. 17. Magnesium hydroxide reduces the levels or effects of sotorasib by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. If co-administration with an acid-reducing agent cannot be avoided, sotorasib should be administered 4 hours before or 10 hours after a locally-acting antacid. 18. Spironolactone increases the levels of magnesium hydroxide by decreasing renal clearance. This interaction is considered minor, and its clinical significance is unknown. 19. Streptomycin increases the renal clearance of magnesium hydroxide, thereby reducing its levels. This interaction is considered minor, and its clinical significance is unknown. 20. Mineral oil decreases the levels of sulfadiazine, sulfamethoxazole, and sulfisoxazole by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. These interactions apply only to the oral forms of both agents. The clinical significance of these interactions is unknown. 21. Magnesium hydroxide reduces the levels of tetracycline by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Co-administration should be avoided, and alternative drugs should be considered. 22. Tobramycin increases the renal clearance of magnesium hydroxide, thereby reducing its levels. This interaction is considered minor, and its clinical significance is unknown. 23. Torsemide increases the renal clearance of magnesium hydroxide, thereby reducing its levels. This interaction is considered minor, and its clinical significance is unknown. 24. Triamterene increases the levels of magnesium hydroxide by decreasing renal clearance. This interaction is considered minor, and its clinical significance is unknown. 25. Magnesium hydroxide reduces the levels or effects of vismodegib by altering its solubility due to increased gastric pH, which reduces bioavailability. The effect on efficacy is unknown. Caution is advised, and close monitoring is required. 26. Mineral oil decreases the levels of vitamins A, D, E, and K1 (phytomenadione) by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. These interactions apply only to the oral forms of both agents. The clinical significance of these interactions is unknown. Concomitant use of mineral oil and vitamin D supplements should be avoided to prevent decreased absorption of vitamin D. Vitamin D can increase serum magnesium concentrations, particularly in patients with renal impairment. Combined use of vitamin D and magnesium-containing products should be avoided in patients with chronic renal failure. 27. Adverse effects of magnesium hydroxide and mineral oil include hypotension, respiratory depression, lipid pneumonia (if taken while reclined), excessive bowel activity, abdominal cramping, electrolyte imbalance, muscle weakness, anal pruritus and irritation, and laxative dependence (avoid chronic use). Contraindications include existing electrolyte imbalance, symptoms of appendicitis, acute surgical abdomen, fecal impaction, intestinal obstruction or perforation, dysphagia, bedridden status, co-administration with stool softeners in children under 6 years, hypersensitivity to the drug or formulation components, renal insufficiency, and magnesium-restricted diets. If taken at bedtime, patients should not recline to avoid aspiration of oil droplets. Administration within 2 hours of meals should be avoided as it may interfere with nutrient and vitamin absorption. Caution is advised in patients with severe renal impairment. 28. Pregnancy Category: Mineral oil is Category C, and magnesium hydroxide is Category B. Lactation: Mineral oil should be used cautiously during breastfeeding as it is unknown whether it is excreted into breast milk.
